text: I took Computer Networks mainly to fit into my schedule, not out of some big interest in the topic, and that shaped how I approached it from day one. The material felt accessible at times, and the basic concepts were manageable, but the course still wore me out more than I expected—especially with the pace ramping up after each new topic. Dr. Chen’s delivery varies week to week; some lectures click and others feel like you’re chasing explanations, which made the weeks feel uneven. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which was a small relief when I was juggling other courses, but feedback came sparsely and often felt late, so I never quite knew where I stood before the next assignment. I found the course works best if you have a study group to bounce ideas off, since solo review of the lecture slides didn’t quite cut it. I earned a failing grade, yet I still have mixed feelings because some parts of the content were genuinely challenging in a way that stretched my understanding, even if the overall outcome was rough. Compared to another intro course I did this term, this one felt more exhausting but had some fair assessment moments that kept me pushing through. Overall, I’m not sure I’d recommend it, though I can see why someone else might find it doable with the right rhythm.

I stuck with Cyber Security Basics only when I needed it, and the lead-in theory never clicked for me, though the explanations were clear. Early on I kept getting tangled in hash stuff, and the weird mix of few but heavy deadlines left me frustrated but still fair about the effort.

I’m new to this discipline and learning the basics, and Data Structures felt like a required hurdle more than a doorway to real understanding. The assessments are exhausting and feel predictably overbearing for someone still grappling with the basics; even when I think I’ve nailed a concept, the next assignment spotlights tiny edge cases and drags the energy out of me. The course pretends to be about relevance to real coding, but the problems often read like abstract puzzles that don’t map clearly to what I’ll actually do in a specialization, which left me wondering why some topics were foregrounded while others seemed buried. Group work can add value when you get a solid team, yet I watched a few peers carry the load while I scrambled to keep up, which didn’t help my confidence. Feedback is sparse until it’s almost too late, and the email support drags on during deadlines, so the moment I needed guidance most I just got a slow pushback. There was one practical project—the tiny hash-table with separate chaining—that felt doable and tangible, but the overall design of the assessments still wore me out and left me feeling like I had to push through more than learn.

I took Database Systems mainly because I needed it for my specialization, and I’m new to the discipline, so I was trying to fill in gaps without getting overwhelmed. Prof. Haddad is solid enough, and the material is clearly aimed at giving you the basics you need, which helped me keep up while juggling two other demanding courses. The platform quirks were a real annoyance—occasional login hiccups and weird file sync timing made some weeks stressful, even when the content was straightforward. The coursework is very assignment-heavy with frequent deadlines, which I appreciated for keeping me on track, but it also meant I fought to balance it with everything else, especially when I was still learning the basics. I found the prerequisite fit better than I expected, and I felt steadier about the core ideas than I would have in a looser intro, though the collaboration expectations felt unclear and I didn’t always know who was supposed to drive the group work. If there’s one concrete memory, it’s the midterm where you had to design a simple schema and justify it in short notes, which showed the practical application clearly, even if the exam felt fair in that pressure-filled way. I wouldn’t take it again, but it did push me forward, and I learned more than I thought I would, despite the stress.

I signed up hoping Data Structures would pay off in industry work, but the delivery felt uneven week to week, and by midterm I’d glazed over while the grading got murky. TAs were helpful, and I liked the instructor, but the overall vibe was still rough.

Prolly the workload felt fine and I kept up, but the tool setup took ages and the payoff wasn’t worth the extra hassle; grading was opaque enough, and the exams felt harsher than the effort, especially compared to another course this term. Prof. Cohen, TAs were responsive though.

I’m new to the field, and I took Operating Systems mainly out of curiosity and the sense that I should start somewhere solid. The lectures were clear and the pacing felt reasonable, which helped me grasp the basics even when I was juggling a bunch of other classes. The workload was fair for a beginner, and I appreciated how the weekly labs tied into the lectures, especially the hands-on exercises that forced me to think about processes and memory management beyond theory. A standout memory: I walked in with total confusion about scheduling on day one, and the quick, concrete example in class helped me finally grok the idea, even if I still wasn’t perfect by the midterm. That midterm felt like it reflected real effort rather than a trick question, though the rubric was vague enough to leave me unsure about how the partial credits were awarded. The platform quirks created avoidable stress—some tool quirks and the way submissions streamed in timing-wise were annoying, and I wish the grading criteria were clearer. Overall, I’d say it fits best if you’ve already seen adjacent material; otherwise you’ll be chasing concepts in parallel with the coursework.

Machine Learning was a solid fit for my late-evening study rhythm, but it felt unevenly paced for a middle-of-the-semester sprint when my schedule was already tensed up. The lectures were clear and the pacing reasonable on the surface, though I mostly dipped into the slides and the occasional discussion thread rather than watching every live session, since I’d squeeze in coding practice between other classes. For someone with a strong coding background but weaker theory, the prerequisite material was mostly helpful and the course built on it, but the big project and the high-stakes exams loomed in a way that kept me hopping between forums, office hours, and a couple of TAs who could sanity-check a convolutional idea or a gradient issue. Feedback arrived sporadically, often after I’d already made a lot of progress or realized I’d veered off course, which felt like a letdown when I needed guidance mid-crunch. The project had a concrete deliverable, a notebook plus a write-up, and I still remember debugging a stubborn misalignment between my data split and the model’s expectations late in the week, which felt like a mini-ordeal. All told, it’s doable, just not as smooth as I hoped during that rough midterm stretch.

Took Operating Systems while working full-time in my first semester, and I often fell behind until deadlines, then caught up; the grading rubric felt vague and feedback was sparse, which made a late curve feel quasi-necessary. The course seems to run better with a study group.

I took Operating Systems in the middle of a brutal semester and it felt more like a slog than a help. The tool setup alone ate a chunk of time, and I felt like I needed more prior background than the catalog promises; I barely passed after struggling most of the term. Still, I did find some practical usefulness for industry work, even if the lectures and assessments didn’t align well and peers helped more than the staff.

I took Linear Algebra with Dr. Park while juggling a full-time job, and I’ll admit the coursework felt doable at first but ramped up fast, especially once the specialization needed it. The recorded lectures helped when I was tired after shifts, but they felt dry, and the few assessments mattered a lot, so I dreaded deadlines that sneaked up; I fell behind and only caught up right before the due date. First semester in the program, and I’m still fuzzy on how the exams line up with what we covered in lectures, so I can’t say it felt perfectly fair, but I’m not sure that’s a dealbreaker either. I’m comfortable with proofs, not so much systems work, which didn’t help when we had to map theoretical ideas to the DB stuff, and the group work sometimes clicked when the team actually communicated, but tanked when one person disappeared. Office hours saved me a few times, and I remember an early lecture confusion about normalization that kind of stuck with me and shaped the term, even though the feedback only started showing up late. The project with the small SQL tooling was the moment I realized the pace is real, yet I still feel I’m asking the right questions too late.

Honestly, the Machine Learning course felt like I was catching my breath after a long reset, since I’m a returning student who still feels rusty in spots. I kept up with nearly every lecture, partly because I needed it for the specialization, but the software stack was rough at first and only became manageable after a few weeks of tinkering with the environment. The conceptual explanations were solid enough to ground me, yet the real-world examples were thin, which left me chasing a few “aha” moments during the assignments. The group work adds value when the team functions well, but when the collaboration flopped mid‑term I felt the drag, and instructions often left too much to interpretation, which fed my fatigue. I’d say the biggest friction was administrative: deadlines that seemed to move or blur just enough to require extra back-and-forth with the TA. There’s a lingering sense that the course gave me useful tools, but I’m not sure I’d re-enroll if I could skip it, even though it helped me push through the first semester and regain a bit of confidence. It’s not tidy, but it’s real.

I’m a returning student who feels rusty, and Cyber Security Basics under Prof. Alvarez dragged on in the summer term with compressed pacing; the platform quirks and vague rubric left me stressed, but I’ll admit some parts were useful even if the grading felt off.

I took Machine Learning in my last semester, mainly out of curiosity more than anything else, and I did end up learning a lot even though the whole experience felt a bit uneven. The professor’s explanations were strong on concepts, but the actual examples and hands-on demos were thin, so I often had to piece things together from forums and the TAs during office hours. Attendance was low-key practical for me—I used the materials selectively when I needed a quick reference, not to follow every lecture step by step. The grading felt pretty opaque at times: feedback would show up late on some assignments, which undercut its usefulness, and a couple of quizzes seemed to hinge on tiny implementation quirks rather than core understanding. I came in with a strong coding background but weaker theory, so I stuck to the parts I could translate into code and skimmed the rest, which left me frustrated at moments. There was also a heavy setup hurdle with the tooling, and it took more effort than the payoff, which cooled my enthusiasm a bit, especially since I was comparing it to another course from the same term that felt more practical day-to-day. Despite that, the late-semester turning point clicked for me in a way I didn’t expect, anchoring the whole course in a memory that I’ll carry into grad school applications.

I’m a returning student who felt a bit rusty, but the Computer Networks class still kept my interest alive, especially as I tried to fit study around short evening sessions between meetings. The LMS and submission flow were smooth enough that I didn’t chase down glitches after a long day, and the prerequisite material lined up with what we actually covered, so I wasn’t wandering in blind. Slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I found myself re-reading the same definitions to make sure I wasn’t missing something when I was juggling other tasks. The middle of a heavy semester made the pace feel steady rather than frantic, which helped, though the grading rubric often felt vague in places, like it could have been clearer about what counts for partial credit on design questions. One concrete quirk stuck with me: the weekly mini-projects lived in a small corner of the LMS with odd naming—nothing dangerous, just enough to stumble over once or twice and then adjust. Overall I’d say I’d recommend it, but only if you come prepared to bridge a few gaps on your own and keep moving between study blocks.

The Machine Learning course was solid in how it kept me moving forward, even though I was juggling it with another tough class and felt a bit rusty as a returning student. It starts approachable but ramps up fast, and the few big assessments mattered more than I expected. The platform quirks drove me nuts and email support felt slow when deadlines loomed, so I’d only recommend it if you come in with a plan and a bit of prep time.

Taking Database Systems as an advanced elective was worth it for the practical side, even though I came in with a strong coding background but weak theory. Prof. Haddad kept the pace brisk, and I found the hands-on parts surprisingly useful: I used the materials selectively, digging into indexing and query planning when I hit a real project bottleneck rather than trying to ingest everything at once. The course works better if you have a study group, since several of the tricky topics only clicked after hashing them out with peers. One concrete friction point for me was tooling and platform hiccups during deadline weeks, which really amplified the stress when the clock was ticking. Instructions left too much room for interpretation, so I often relied on a quick chat in office hours to confirm what counted as a submission-ready artifact. Scores arrived fast, but the explanations felt thin, so I had to infer how a borderline solution was evaluated. I managed the workload alongside full-time work, and I appreciated the fair yet exhausting assessment that still pushed me to stay sharp. I’ll remember the late-night forum thread where Haddad weighed in on a tricky join optimization and clarified the grading quirk.

Data Structures was a required hurdle, and juggling it with other heavy courses left me relying on late-night slide skim. The turning point was realizing the peer-discussion chats clarified concepts better than the official materials, while email support stretched when deadlines loomed.

I’m in the middle of a brutal semester and took Computer Networks more as a necessary credit than a passion project, so I used the materials when I needed them and skimmed the rest. The lectures feel dry even though the concepts click when I actually sit down with the slides, and I’m stuck with a sense that the course assumes more prior knowledge than what was advertised. Grading comments show real detail, but they arrive late enough to miss a few quick fixes, which is frustrating when you’re balancing a full-time job. I did like the LMS flow and how submissions go through smoothly, and I remember one office-hours chat where I finally got a straightforward explanation for a routing question, which stuck with me—just not enough to rescue the overall vibe.

Taking Linear Algebra mainly felt like a schedule fit more than a genuine interest spike, since this was a required course for the track and I needed it to line up with other classes. Prof. Alvarez delivered solid conceptual explanations, but the examples were thin and I kept hitting moments where I understood the idea in theory yet struggled to see how to apply it on a problem set, which made the turning point late in the term feel almost like a relief more than a breakthrough. The platform quirks and some sloppy communication around deadlines added unnecessary stress, so I ended up scrambling at the end of weeks when a single message would have clarified things; it didn’t help that the prerequisites feel like they work best if you already know adjacent material. I remember one late-semester exam where the questions teased you with a neat idea, but then the formatting glitch ate time and I barely finished, which stuck with me more than the content itself. Compared to another course from the same term, this one felt sturdier in theory but messier in practice, and I’m not sure whether I’d recommend it, even though I did learn a lot—just not with a smooth experience.

Cyber Security Basics dragged me through the last semester, and I’m genuinely curious why I stuck with it at all. The workload felt manageable in bursts, but the way the material ramps up quickly at week three left me scrambling more than once, so I barely kept my head above water. I used the lecture notes and demos only when I needed them, and the software stack started rough but ended up tolerable, which helped a bit. I remember one office-hours chat where I showed a weird config issue and the TA walked me through a workaround, which kept my grade from tanking after a late assignment. Instructions sometimes left too much to interpretation, and emails about deadlines were slow, but I still learned enough to feel oddly proud when I finally passed.

I took Data Structures in my first semester because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and the lectures were genuinely clear—the lecturer kept concepts grounded and the examples clicked. I appreciated that the TAs were responsive and practical, often guiding me through tricky data-flow questions in forums and during office hours, which helped fill gaps the prerequisite didn’t fully cover. The tooling setup, though, was a pain—npm quirks and a brittle project scaffold slowed me down more than I’d expect in an advanced elective. Our project and report-heavy workload kept piling up, deadlines stacking up in ways I didn’t anticipate, and I ended up rushing sections to meet the curve, even though I learned a lot from the deeper dives. I’ll admit the experience was rough, but I did walk away with real skills that feel job-ready.

Dr. Miller was clear most of the time, and I kept up with nearly every lecture in Computer Networks, but the grading comments came too late to help, and tooling issues during the week of the big exam lingered; one memorable week was that tricky TCP practice project.

Calculus II with Dr. Park was tougher than I expected but still doable given the workload—lots of assignments and frequent deadlines kept me on my toes, even though I mostly relied on recordings and notes. The prereqs start accessible but ramp up sharply, and I found the feedback sparse until it felt too late; I did hit a few useful office hours and chatted with a TA about a late-night coding snag, which helped.

Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez felt fine clocking in nearly every lecture, but I’m a returning student who felt rusty and wished the pace matched the lectures better; the sparse feedback came too late and the mix of assessments exhausted me even though the workload wasn’t crazy, especially compared to my other course this term.

I took Data Structures as an advanced elective while juggling a full-time job, and it was a slog more than I expected. The tooling and submission flow were smooth, but the actual work felt heavy and the workload kept piling up despite short evening study sessions I forced around dinners and commutes. I fell behind and caught up around deadlines, which meant cramming the last few chapters before the big midterm and barely scraping a pass because most assessments mattered a lot and there weren’t many of them. The collaboration expectations felt unclear, so I ending up doing a lot solo work even when I wished for some real pair programming, and I kept thinking this was a prerequisite course in disguise, easier than this pace. Feedback came in slowly, with detailed grading comments only after I’d already moved on to the next assignment, which didn’t help when I needed guidance right away. The LMS and submission flow stayed steady, but the real stress was the sequence of hard problems that didn’t align well with a late-night window. A turning point late in the term finally clicking a data structure idea helped me breathe, but I still wouldn’t call the experience smooth.

Took Calculus II with Prof. Rios while juggling a full-time job, and the weeks felt uneven; the office hours saved me more than once, but the prerequisites hit me hard—felt like more prior knowledge was assumed than advertised.

I’m in my last semester and juggling a full-time job, so I fell behind in the Computer Networks course and ended up sprinting to catch up around the deadlines, which left me with a nagging sense of churn rather than steady progress. Dr. Miller is approachable and the peer help in our cohort surprisingly carried more weight than any instructor response, which helped when I was stuck on the TCP congestion window timings. The assessment mix felt misaligned with the lectures: we had a heavy project component and a couple of quick quizzes that didn’t map neatly to what we’d covered in class, so I ended up guessing through some of the practical bits. Practical application was the hardest pill to swallow, especially since the tooling didn’t feel obviously user-friendly for someone who’s already steeped in adjacent material; I kept wishing there was a clearer roadmap showing how the lab tasks tied to real deployments. I did appreciate the group work when our team clicked, but relying on someone else to pull extra weight added stress given my time constraints. A late-semester turning point was the moment I realized I needed to prioritize the core concepts over trying to master every tool, and that realization came with mixed relief and frustration.

I took Database Systems mainly because I needed it for a specialization, and I appreciated how supportive the instructor staff could be when I reached out during office hours. The pacing felt workable most weeks, especially since I usually fit study around short evening sessions and relied on recordings and notes more than live lectures. I have a strong coding background but weaker theory, so the way they assumed more prior knowledge than advertised left me juggling concepts; the course finally clicked when I paired up with a study group, which helped me push through the dense parts. The assessments were heavy in the sense that the reports dragged on and the rubric felt vague, which made it hard to gauge what exactly counted, even though I thought the questions were fair. Time pressure was still manageable most weeks, but the workload was exhausting because the same material kept resurfacing in different report formats. Collaborating with peers helped, but solo work often felt like I was chasing the same clarifications in multiple drafts. The whole thing pales in comparison to my easier prerequisite, and I sometimes wished the course had clearer milestones; still, the support kept me going.

I’m in my first semester, juggling a full-time job, and I tried to fit Machine Learning around short evening sessions with Prof. Alvarez. The lectures are clear and the pacing isn’t bad, but the grading rubric still feels vague, which has left me guessing about what exactly earns points and where I went wrong on the latest assignment. The software stack started rough for me at first, though it smooths out after a couple of weeks, and the TAs are reasonably responsive and practical when I hit a wall. I compare this to another course from the same term, which had tighter rubric guidance but tougher deadlines, and I found myself wishing for a bit more precision here. Overall, I’ve softened my initial frustration, but the friction around grading sticks with me.

This last term in OS felt like I was trying to redo a lot of rusty muscle memory while the deadlines stacked up in ways I didn’t expect. Prof. Rios is solid in office hours—the rescue moments that actually kept me from throwing in the towel—but the grading rubric felt vague and left me guessing what mattered most for the final. The group work could click when the team functioned, but otherwise it dragged; I liked having a few practical tasks, like that mini kernel assignment, but the pace kept me neutral rather than energized. I’m glad I made it the main focus course, yet I wouldn’t recommend it without a clear heads-up about the rubric and timing.

I took Database Systems mostly because it was required, and I’m glad I survived. The peer discussion saved me more than the official materials, since the forums could be dismissive and the recorded lectures felt dry, especially during a rough mid-semester crunch. Tooling problems made deadlines feel worse, and I’d still not take it again, but I’ll admit I learned enough to pass and hatched a few practical ideas I’ll actually use, if only narrowly.

I’m in my last semester and juggling a few heavy courses, so Cyber Security Basics felt like a useful check-in with industry stuff, even though my attendance faded mid-semester as other deadlines piled up. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped when I managed to stay on top of things, but the collaboration expectations were unclear and I often didn’t know who was supposed to do what. TAs were responsive and practical when I asked for quick pivots, and the course did build well on the prerequisites, but I didn’t always enjoy it as much as I expected—still, I ended up appreciating the practical angle more than the teaching moments. A late-semester turning point around a capstone-style exercise stood out, anchoring this memory even as I drifted in and out of engagement.

Taking Cyber Security Basics this year fit my schedule more than my curiosity, but I felt a bit hand-wavy about the grading rubric and the overall pace; I relied on office hours with Prof. Alvarez and the TA for clarity, yet feedback came sparse until it felt late.

I went into Linear Algebra expecting to freshen up basics, and it felt like the main focus all term, especially with the project-heavy workload. Prof. Cohen is organized, but the tooling setup and email support during crunch deadlines were frustrating. The course works better if you have a study group; my rusty self finally clicked something after a quick office-hours chat about the eigenvalue assignment, but I barely scraped by.

Data Structures was solid enough to keep me engaged through my last semester before graduation, even though I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics. The lectures flowed clearly and the pacing felt reasonable, plus the TAs were responsive and practical, which helped when I kept up with nearly every lecture. I appreciated quick feedback so I could adjust on the fly, though the platform quirks did create some avoidable stress during assignments. The assessment felt fair but exhausting, like there was a lot of grind to prove the same concepts, and I left with a solid B that matched the effort I put in. A small project with a shared code snippet stood out, but honestly the grind lingered longer than I expected.

Summer term moved fast, and I kept up with nearly every lecture, but I’d get exhausted by the end of the week and wonder if the pacing was really built for consistency. Dr. Park’s project-heavy setup meant the high-stakes exams loomed, and I remember that early confusion about eigenvectors shaping how I approached everything after—plus feedback arriving too late to actually help. The expectations around collaboration felt murky, and it often seemed the prerequisites assumed more prior knowledge than advertised.

Overall I’d say it helped me wrap my head around the concepts, but the pace in the summer term felt tight and the examples were thin. I used the materials only when needed, and the emails about deadlines dragged a bit.

I’m not sure I’d take Cyber Security Basics again, but I did learn some useful things, especially the broad ideas about threat models and risk phrasing. Prof. Cohen explains concepts well, and when he walks through a scenario in class it sticks—it's just the real-world examples that felt thin, like we were talking in theory without enough concrete cases. Most of my time relied on the recordings and notes because the live sessions were tricky to follow when the tooling hiccups hit and deadlines slipped; the platform plus a few sudden tool outages turned a lot of weeks into frantic, last-minute pushes. The project-heavy setup and high-stakes exams mean you’re always juggling, and I often felt behind because the feedback loop was slow—email support dragged when deadlines loomed, so I had to stay oddly paranoid about every submission. I do remember a detailed office-hours chat where I showed a partial risk assessment map and the professor gave a blunt nudge about focusing on the core asset of the model, which helped a bit. Overall, useful but not enjoyable, and I’d still broadly recommend it to someone who can tolerate the rough edges.

The Computer Networks course started strong for me, and the assessment design kept me on my toes without wiping me out, even as the pacing got tight during the summer term. I remember firing off questions by email and feeling the support move slower when deadlines loomed, plus a rough first-week toolset that somehow got manageable later. I wish the week-to-week rhythm felt more solid, and I learned early on that I work better if I study with a group, because solo drafts wore me out.

I’m glad the course was organized well enough to keep me in hand, since juggling a full-time job and limited weekly study time during the summer term meant I needed a predictable rhythm. The grading rubric felt vague at first, and the platform quirks added unnecessary stress, especially with the frequent deadlines piling up in a compressed pace. The feedback was thorough but arrived later than I’d hoped, which didn’t help when I was scrambling to adjust for the next assignment. I still, weirdly, learned something tangible, like when our project required a quick pivot to a different library midstream, but I left with a mix of relief and fatigue, and I’m not sure I’d want this pacing again.

Database Systems was one of those required-but-not-quite-wreathed-with-glory courses for the track, and I came in with a decent coding background but fuzzy theory and lots of questions about how the pieces actually fit. The fastest way I felt I could keep up was to dive into the peer discussions; honestly, those chats helped more than the official materials, especially when the lecture slides hopped between topics and I fell behind around deadlines. Feedback came quickly enough to adjust some days, but there were times when it felt like the grading and the deadlines stacked up unexpectedly and I’d only realize after I’d already missed a chance to fix something. The prerequisites assume a bit more background than I expected, which left me scrambling to connect concepts, even though I kept thinking I should be able to handle it given a strong code background. I did a late sprint on the big project too, and the one practical database design assignment reminded me how the theory still doesn’t snap into place until you see the concrete constraints. All in all, I’m mostly calm about it, just not fully confident that the pace always lined up with where I was in the material. The one thing that stands out and sticks is the back-and-forth with peers; that’s the real takeaway here.

I took the Advanced OS elective with Dr. Singh, and I’m torn but basically glad I stuck with it, even though I don’t know if the grade really proves I understood everything. I mostly relied on the recordings and notes, because the live sessions felt dry and a bit hard to follow, especially when the examples droned on. The tooling glitches during deadline weeks didn’t help—turning in a late assignment because the platform froze felt like a recurring punchline, not something you can plan around. The forums helped at times, but there were days when the responses sounded short and dismissive, which didn’t exactly push me forward. Most of the work was solo, which fits my pace, but I kept thinking back to the other course from the same term that gave clearer feedback and less fatigue, even if it wasn’t perfect either. A late-semester turning point, a practical memory of debugging a race condition in a simulated scheduler, sticks out as the moment I felt the material clicked—yet I still left with mixed feelings, unsure if the C reflected my true understanding or just the semester’s grind.

I signed up for Linear Algebra thinking it would be the main focus of my term, and it started off pretty engaging with Prof. Haddad, but the attendance faded for me mid-semester once the projects piled up and the midterms loomed. The software stack we used—at first rough, then more manageable after some fiddling—felt like a constant hurdle, especially during setup, which was frustrating and ate into study time. The course leaned hard on a project-heavy workflow and high-stakes exams, and I ended up feeling like you needed more prior toolkit than was advertised to keep pace, which was a real mismatch for where I was at. I managed to land an A after a curve, but a lot of that came from grinding through the later assignments and cramming for the final, not from any shining clarity in the early lectures. There was one deadline spike that stuck with me—an on-the-fly data transformation in the project that I botched until I recovered with a late-night debugging sprint—and it summed up the whole term for me: rewarding when it clicked, but the friction was real. Not sure I’d definitively recommend it, given all the rough edges and the mid-semester crunch.

Calculus II was a mid-program core debacle for me, since I’m juggling a full-time job and can only carve out small weekly study blocks, and I still ended up with a failed grade but mixed feelings about the course. The lecturer was genuinely positive and clear when he spoke, and the occasional practical example he offered felt grounded, which helped during the late-semester crunch. The feedback quality bounced a lot by assignment—some comments were timely and useful, others felt vague or late enough that I couldn’t salvage the problem set. The grading rubric, honestly, seemed vague enough to make me doubt what exactly counted as a “step” in the proofs, and that friction lingered through the last exam. Peer discussion helped more than the official materials, especially when we swapped quick solution sketches before the weekly quizzes; the TAs were responsive and pragmatic, which saved me a few times. By the end, I kept comparing it to prerequisites that felt easier, and I kept wishing the course would be a little more predictable about deadlines or a clearer path through the tricky substitution stuff, which was enough to keep me turning through the material, even if the turning point didn’t land neatly.

When I started Data Structures with Prof. Alvarez, I was new to the basics and found the short evening sessions fit my schedule, though the recorded lectures feel dry. The assignment-heavy pace with frequent deadlines left me juggling tasks, and email support was slow right when I needed feedback before a deadline. I remember an early confusion about pointers that shaped how I approached later topics anyway. Overall, it’s a mixed ride.

Taking Database Systems as an advanced elective while juggling a full-time job left me feeling rusty and a bit cautious about my progress, especially since I needed it for a specialization. The software stack started rough for me at first—SQL tooling and a few ORM quirks felt like stumbling blocks until I settled into the rhythm, and the later weeks were more manageable. My weekly study time was limited, so I relied on the materials only when I needed them, and that worked until the big assignment drops with frequent deadlines started piling up; I still felt I had the right rough understanding, but I’m not sure the grade in the C band fully reflected what I grasped during the semester. Dr. Chen’s delivery is serviceable: slides get you through the key ideas, but they aren’t memorable, and the in-class moments didn’t really lock in concepts for me, especially with the time pressure from the workload. One small incident sticks—getting an extension on a minor component of the project and realizing the rest of the team didn’t share that pressure—made the reality hit hard, but I kept pushing. Overall, I’d say I wouldn’t take it again, even though it helped me summarize core data structures under real-world time constraints.

I dragged through Data Structures in my last semester, using the materials only when I had to and still somehow barely passed after wrestling with the graded tasks most of the term. I liked the instructor, but the grading felt dry and inconsistent, and the recorded lectures were helpful but not engaging enough to sustain me—the class mostly felt like everyone else’s questions carried the day.

Peer discussion saved a lot—the group I sat with unpacked tricky chain rule problems faster than the official notes, and that helped me keep a B without cramming. The admin stuff left too much wiggle room, but office hours were a rescue; I’d go with a concrete question and walk away with a clear path for the next assignment.

Starting in Cyber Security Basics, I knew the first semester would be busy, but the workload felt heavy for someone juggling a full-time job and limited weekly study time. The assignment-heavy pace with frequent deadlines didn’t help my motivation stay steady, and the tooling setup with Dr. Singh was more frustrating than helpful at times. Some feedback on a few tasks came quickly, but other times it felt delayed and uneven, which didn’t help me keep track of what to fix next.

Dr. Chen is genuinely solid, especially for someone like me in the first semester who came in hoping Linear Algebra would click quickly. I leaned on the recordings and notes a lot, but the live lectures still helped when I hit a rough mid-semester crunch and needed a quick sense-check—office hours became the rescue for me. The course did fill in prerequisite gaps better than I expected, though the feedback often felt sparse until it was almost too late, which left me scrambling to adjust for the next deadline. One concrete hiccup: a project prompt that required interpreting a vague instruction; I kept re-reading the rubric and still wasn’t sure I was aligned. By the end, I wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push me to rethink how I study, and that turning point changed how I approached the rest of the term.

I took Operating Systems this summer, mostly juggling it after my full-time job, and the short evening sessions fit my week but left me scrambling to keep up when the pacing suddenly tightened. The lectures are fine enough to follow, but the slides don’t stick in memory and I often left the room thinking I understood the concept and realized an hour later I didn’t, which didn’t help when the next topic relied on it. The workload felt reasonable for a compressed term, and the way it asked us to apply ideas in quick mini-assignments kind of matched my limited study windows, even if I occasionally wished for a bit more structure to plan around the deadlines. I appreciated that the course filled in some prerequisite gaps better than I expected, especially around process synchronization, but the platform quirks—odd auto-saving and a flaky quiz timer—added avoidable stress during crunch weeks. Email support was slow right when deadlines crept up, which was frustrating, though I kept going because I was genuinely curious about the topic. I’d still recommend it to others who can carve out steady evenings and aren’t hoping for a memorable slide deck, and I’d probably take it again if I needed a refresher.

Cyber Security Basics held its place in the middle of a heavy semester, and I stuck with it mainly because the schedule fit better than my interest in the material. I’m comfortable with proofs but not with the systems side, so the turn toward hands-on labs left me feeling a step behind. The fast-ish score returns are real, but the explanations never quite filled in the why, and by the time feedback lands it’s too late to adjust for the next deadline. One concrete moment that sticks: the midterm felt like a rapid-fire mix of questions from different topics, and I was scrambling between full-time work and study notes. I’m not sure I’d recommend it, yet I did learn a few practical bits I’ll probably keep.

Data Structures with Prof. Rios moved at a steady pace, which helped despite my confusion early on. I mostly used the materials when I knew I needed them, and the LMS submission flow was smooth, though the feedback felt quick and a bit thin. The report-heavy tasks dragged and I’m not sure the grade reflected my understanding, especially compared to a simpler prerequisite.

I came into Database Systems this summer feeling a bit rusty, and the course kept a steady pace that wasn’t as frantic as I feared. The quick feedback helped me realign after a rough week, and the peer discussion somehow made the official materials feel a bit thinner but more approachable. The lectures themselves were useful when I rewatched them, but they dragged a bit dry on first listen. The project a week before the final felt heavy but fair, and I remember an exam week where I finally put together a practical query plan that clicked, which stood out as a memory anchor. I’m not fully sure I’d recommend it, but it did push me to stretch despite the compressed pacing.

The feedback is detailed but sometimes arrives late, which stings when you’re juggling deadlines, and the admin side sometimes feels sloppy enough that I double-checked before relying on a policy. Still, I’d recommend it only if you’re prepared to push through the constant late nights for a turning-point moment I remember near the midterm where everything clicked for a minute.

This summer, I treated Machine Learning as my main focus while juggling a full-time job, so I barely had space for anything else, and the pacing felt brutally compressed. It’s very assignment-heavy, with frequent deadlines that kept me sprinting the whole term, and I found the support channel mostly people helping each other more than staff. My final grade sits in that C range, and I’m unsure if it truly reflected what I understood; I felt unsure about whether I could explain the material to someone else, given the pace and the prerequisites.

Summer term in OS with Dr. Miller felt practical but tiring; slides are fine but not memorable, and the pace was brutal for someone who hadn’t brushed up on adjacent topics. One memorable week—the exam on process scheduling—stuck, but I still found the material marginally useful for industry work.

I fell behind early, then scrambled to catch up around deadlines, and that pattern made the few assessments feel like make-or-break moments—each one mattered a lot, even though there weren’t many checks along the way. The fast feedback on scores was there, but explanations were skimpy, kind of like “you got it wrong because X” without the “how to fix Y next time” guidance I actually needed. I think it’s best if you already know adjacent material; it helps, otherwise the course feels like it’s trying to be helpful while still assuming you’re reading between the lines. My memory anchor is an early confusion about process states that shaped how I approached every later topic, which is a frustrating but oddly useful reminder to stay cautious about taking everything at face value. I would only recommend it with serious preparation and a willingness to treat it as the main focus of the term.

I remember one week around the TCP timing analysis where I stayed up too late and still wasn’t confident I’d captured the right nuance, a memory that sticks because it felt like the course wanted curves of insight but delivered queues of output. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend it, though there is value if you’re willing to push through the gaps and rely on your own pace.

The project-heavy vibe and high-stakes exams pushed me to keep up, but the feedback came too late to actually help midcourse, so I ended up debugging my own mistakes after the fact and regretting some timing on my side. I recall one concrete moment: a final group of data-structure implementations where I used a persistent map approach I hadn’t practiced before, and the grading quirk of a late-graded quiz that felt punitive even though the rubric was fair. Compared to another course from the same term, this one felt more exhausting despite similar workload, and I sometimes felt the daily grind of deadlines stacking up with another hard class. Overall, it’s not tidy, but I did learn to navigate under pressure even if the path was rough.

I’m in my last semester and took Computer Networks mainly because it’s a specialization requirement, and I threw myself into it as the main focus of the term. The class felt like mid-program core that assumed I already knew more than I did, so I spent extra evenings mapping the lecture notes to the project work and worrying about gaps. The TAs were practical and quick to respond when I asked about the routing table assignment, but the grading rubric still felt vague, like there was a hidden standard I wasn’t hitting. The project-heavy setup kept my stress high with a couple of high-stakes exams, and I’m still torn about whether I’d recommend it; it helped in some stubborn ways, but I wouldn’t take it again if I had a choice.

Calculus II felt like it starts accessible but ramps up fast, so I fit study around short evening bursts after work. The deadlines stacked up unpredictably, tooling glitches made some weeks worse, and I mainly used slides when really needed.

I signed up for Computer Networks hoping to get a solid grip on the backbone stuff, but I mostly fell back on recordings and notes because the lectures felt open to interpretation and I didn’t quite know what was expected of me. My strongest background is coding, not theory, so the early module about TCP pitfalls and congestion control left me confused instead of empowered, and I remember an initial slide that shrugged off details like timing diagrams as “left as an exercise.” The forums helped sometimes, but a few threads felt curt or dismissive when I asked for concrete examples, which didn’t help when I was scrambling to meet a stack of deadlines that piled up in week three. Grades arrived fast enough, yet the explanations were thin, so I stayed uncertain about what to fix on the next attempt, especially since the peer discussions did a better job clarifying real-world quirks than the official materials. A key turning moment was realizing I’d been muddling through with an early confusion about routing basics, which colored the rest of the term, and now I’m left with mixed feelings and a sense that I didn’t quite “get” the course, even though I learned some practical bits.

Linear Algebra in my first semester was fine for what I needed for the specialization, kept up with nearly every lecture, and the LMS flow was smooth, but I’d still skip it again even though it helped; forums helped, but sometimes felt dismissive when I asked basic questions.

I’m new to the discipline and found myself staring at the basics more often than I’d like, and Dr. Chen’s Computer Networks course didn’t fix that frustration as fast as I hoped. The tool setup felt like a hurdle that didn’t translate into clearer learning—every week a new login dance and a new config quirk, which ate into the time I had to actually work on the network concepts. The assignments pile up with tight deadlines, and the grading rubric is vague enough that I’m unsure what the exact expectations are until after I get the feedback, which is not ideal mid-way through a heavy semester. Still, I’m genuinely enthusiastic about the material when a packet trace finally clicks, even if I can’t honestly recommend it to someone who’s not already wobbling through adjacent topics. I found the summer term rushed and a bit too fast-paced, especially since I’m new to this stuff, but the LMS was smooth and the group work helped when the team clicked; still, feedback often came too late to be useful for the next task.

Taking Operating Systems in the summer term was a mixed bag, especially since I was juggling another hard class at the same time and somehow managed to keep a few study sessions sporadic. I had enough time overall, but my motivation dipped irregularly, so I cherry-picked the materials and only revisited topics when I needed to, which made the pacing feel rough at first. The software stack started rough but got usable after a couple of weeks, once I stopped fighting the setup and just followed the project steps for the virtual environment. The grading rubric always felt vague, and the comments showed up late, which didn’t help when I was scrambling to meet some tight deadlines on the report-heavy assignments. The course is required for my track, and it’s clearly designed to push you into a lot of documentation, but I kept comparing it to the prerequisite that felt easier and simpler to grasp. I wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push some useful skills, and I’m glad the big project helped me push through a few rough days, but I don’t want to relive the timing problems. The ending felt a bit abrupt, with no neat wrap-up to the pacing or the tools we ended up using.

This summer felt like sprinting through a maze: Cyber Security Basics was a required course for my track, compressed into the shortest term and it pushed me to fall behind and then scramble to catch up around deadlines. The report-heavy workload was time-consuming, and I’m not sure the grade in the C band reflected my understanding—I’m still unsure if I actually grokked the material or if I just hustled to meet the rubric. The forums helped at times, but some threads felt dismissive, like if you asked a basic question you got snappy repies instead of patient guidance from TAs or the instructor. Our collaboration expectations were never clear, which meant I often relied on a few scattered peers rather than any formal process, and the communication around policy changes felt sloppy more often than not. A late-semester turning point came when I finally cracked a tricky packet-trace assignment after spending hours re-reading forum tips and a last-minute office hours chat that helped me connect the dots, even if I still can’t decide whether the effort earned the grade. Overall, the tradeoffs—tight pacing, heavy writing, uneven support—make me doubt whether I’d take it again, even though some moments did actually click.

Started the semester eager, but the tooling setup was a slog and the software stack felt rough at first; by midterm I could manage, though collaboration expectations remained oddly vague and email support when deadlines hit was slow.

I took Database Systems in the summer term mainly because it fit my schedule, not because I was itching to dive into theory, and that showed up in how I approached it. Dr. Singh explains concepts clearly enough, but the examples feel a bit thin for someone with a strong coding background and weak theory like mine, so I spent more time filling gaps on my own than I’d expected. The pacing was compressed, which meant I could keep up only if I kept up with the pre-readings, and the tool setup felt like a separate hurdle that didn’t pay off in the learning as much as it demanded time. Feedback tended to be sparse until late, so I’d finish a small assignment and only then see a few notes that felt more like afterthoughts than guidance. By the turning point late in the term, I realized the material would’ve clicked for me if I already knew adjacent topics, which is why I kept thinking, “I wish I’d started this earlier or had a stronger theory foundation.” A project and a midterm format surfaced quirks I’ll remember—like the deadline pattern and how the rubric penalized minor missteps—but the overall takeaway is still useful, even if it wasn’t enjoyable.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Database Systems, but the week jam of deadlines stacked up faster than my brain could process the examples, and I barely squeaked by. The instruction style is solid on the big ideas, but the real-world examples felt thin, so I spent more time guessing than seeing how the concepts fit with actual queries. It’s a required course for the track, and the leap from the easier prerequisite made the prereq feel harsher than advertised, especially when the pace didn’t slow for a midterm that felt more about memory than insight. Peer discussion helped more than the official handouts, and I appreciated that, though I still hit a few wrong turns before the final. Overall I’d recommend broadly, just go in ready to push through the rough patches.

Taking Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez was a ride I didn’t quite see coming, especially since I heard it would be useful for industry work and I tried to pace myself accordingly, but the week-to-week teaching felt uneven and left me scrambling to line up the threads. The tooling setup to actually run the assignments was frustrating from day one, and that friction bled into how I could even start the problem sets, which didn’t help my motivation when the topics themselves built on prerequisites that, yes, do track, but the delivery kept drifting. Some weeks we’d get a crisp example in class, then the next week we’d pivot to something that didn’t seem to connect, and I ended up barely passing after struggling most of the term, which I didn’t expect given this is an advanced elective and the prerequisites sounded clean. The assessment mix felt off compared to lectures, like quizzes and a couple of big projects didn’t quite map to what we actually spent time on, and I’m not sure how transparent the grading was about that. One concrete moment I’ll remember is the weekend before the midterm when a tool crash erased three hours of effort and I had to restart, which summed up a lot of the semester for me.

Overall, I’d say it’s a tough but doable ride in Computer Networks this first semester, especially to squeeze in after a full-time job. The material feels dense and not very friendly for quick revisits, and the heavy assignment load with tight deadlines kept me racing between tasks. TAs are responsive and practical, but setup and tool quirks ate more time than they should, and communication feels a bit sloppy at times.

Taking Linear Algebra as an intro service course fit around my short evening study blocks has been surprisingly workable. Dr. Miller explains concepts with clear intuition, and the discussions with my peers often clarify abstract ideas more than the official materials do, which is a relief after a long workday. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, and I get quick feedback that lets me adjust before the next problem set; that fast turnaround helps a lot given my limited weekly time. My one real frustration is that the live examples feel a bit thin compared to the solid conceptual explanations, and the assessment, while fair, still exhausts me on tight weeks. Still, the mix feels practical for keeping up without burning out.

Calculus II felt useful but not fun, and I chose it mostly to fit my schedule. slides are serviceable, peer discussions saved me when the official materials fell flat, and I still appreciated office hours with Dr. Miller after the midterm; the tooling setup killed a bit of momentum.

Calculus II with Dr. Singh started accessible enough, but the ramp-up hits hard once you get past the first couple of chapters, especially if you’re like me—strong coding instincts and weak theory—so I felt behind even though I could code away knockoffs of homework problems. The lectures were clear and had decent pacing, which helped when I was still catching up, but the workload exploded with constant assignments and deadlines, and I fell behind more than once before deadlines let me surge back. Office hours saved me more than once; I’d crank through a messy data-structure analogy in my head and somehow get redirected, which was a weird relief, since I appreciated the instructor but hated the grading quirk where a lot of partial credit felt inconsistent. I barely passed after struggling most of the term, and there were moments I thought the course would click early on, then felt like my brain hit a wall mid-chapter, so I kept juggling enough to stay afloat. The pattern of rapid-paced problem sets and frequent check-ins kept me chasing momentum, and yeah, I learned a lot, but the pressure machine of that assignment-heavy schedule left me grumpy and tired by the end.

My first semester sucked me in pretty quickly because the lectures were dense but mostly manageable, and I kept up with nearly every one since it fit neatly into my schedule. It’s a mid-program core course, so the material feels like it relies on some adjacent stuff I already knew, and the assessments were heavy and time-consuming, but the quick feedback helped me adjust fast enough. I’d say it’s fair but exhausting, and while I mostly worked solo, I did appreciate a few concrete reminders like the weekly problem sets
